blocks.x: I'll make a note here that we're interviewing Mr. Louis Cottrell at 731 St. Peter Street, and the date is August 25th, 1961, and Ralph Collins is also present. Would you mind stating your full name, if you have a middle name? Yes, Louis Albert Cottrell.
Could you tell us just when you were born and what part of the city and all? March 7, 1911, right on Robertson between DeVayne and St. Philip. I think the address is 915.

On Robertson? On North Robertson. Naturally, everyone remembers your father. That is, the old timers that have told us, mentioned about his important part in music. Is there anything that you could add to your recollections when you were a boy? By the way, I don't even know when your father died. I don't know. We probably have the date someplace, but I forgot. He died on October 17, 1927. 27?
Yeah, he would have been 49. His next coming boy, which would have been December 25th.
So you were about 16 then? 16. Can you tell us if he ever helped you much in music? Had you started? When did you start in music? I started under my father. It was at the age of 10.

He began with the old method, which often you've heard before, with the solfege. It was singing and for ear training. And then after when he thought I was ready to start on the instrument, then he sent me to Lorenzo Tio Jr.

But how long did he work with you on the solfege? The workman was just about nine months. I know Manuel Perez, they say, did that. And the Tio's too would make you sing a long time. And incidentally speaking, Manuel Perez, he is my godfather. Oh, is that right? Yeah, my godfather. Yes, right. He was my godfather. And by the way, the clarinet then was your first instrument? It is. Yeah, the clarinet was my first instrument. Did you ever want to take up drums? Or were you ever curious about them when your father had them around the house? Well, a little curious, but it was so much to love with. That's why I didn't want to buy it. No, no, baby.
And when I first began on the clarinet, because of my fingers being short, I had to use a C clarinet.
Oh, you did?
Yeah.
Like Big Eye Louie, I guess, used for a long time, they say. Mm.

Yeah. They weren't long enough to expand over the B flat on, or the A clarinet, because they were using those too at the same time. So it was a clarinet of Tio's, but he started off on his C. It was the C-inch.
Is that the young Lorenzo Tio, not the old? No, it's the young Lorenzo. The power, the other older teacher.
No, it wasn't the uncle or the father. It was the young Lorenzo Tio.

Before we get into that, I wonder if you could tell us any more about your father, even what kind of a man he was. I mean, we have pictures of him, usually sitting down. We don't know if he was taller than you. Would you say he's taller than you? Well, he was taller than what I am, yes. He looked rather large, but I never knew. He was about six, one or two. Oh, really? Oh, he was tall. Quite tall. He was quite tall. And he looks very much like you. I think his face from the pictures, like in the P. Rone band, very similar.
He was slim according to his height. It made him appear much slimmer than he was. But the man weighed around about 175 to 180 pounds.
How old was he when he died? Did you remember? He was 48 at the time. Were you not old at all?
No, he would have been 49. He's an exploit day.

Today we'd call that a young man. Yes, he certainly would. We think of him as an older man. Some people, even as you know, call him Old Man Cottrell. Yeah. Well, I guess because of you. Not only that.

The reason why they began calling him Old Man Cottrell is when he had gone to Chicago in 1917. And in the first six months when he returned, he had gotten gray. Only about 40 then. No, he wasn't in the 40s then. Not even in the 40s. Yeah. It was just about, say in the late 30s, you see. And we came back and they began calling him Old Man Cottrell from then on, because of getting gray so fast.
I thought it was because, of course, he was one of the great pioneers, early, very early pioneers too. He was among the first pioneers.
And it's often said that he was the originator of the two-beat drumming. And he was among the first one, or rather the first one that began playing traps in the orchestra in New Orleans.
I know at one time a lot of the bands they say didn't even use drum.

Didn't use drum. He was the first one with the John Robichaux band. So he began using drum in the orchestras in New Orleans. It was mostly string ensemble with a few brass instruments of that type. And he was the first one to be used.
Well, I suppose in those days he used the overhead beater on his drums, wasn't he? The foot pedal?

I think he did. I can't remember him with the overhead. I do remember the overhead because up until 29, they still had a lot of fellas that had been using the overhead pedal. But I don't remember my father with overhead. He always had the other foot pedal. Oh, he did? Yeah. One thing he was more of a stylist around here because anything new came out, he was the first one to use.
I knew that. Some people told me once that he used to work for Whirline's or at least they'd have him to try out all their new equipment. He did. Remember anything about that?
Yes, he did. Up until the time that he died in 27, he still was done at Whirline. He was a representative, a salesman for them on the instruments.

Did he ever work in their shop as a repairman or anything of that kind or as a salesman in the store? No, it was just an outside street sale. Yeah. Do you know anything about his drum set, his latest one? Of course, you knew about the last one you did.

The latest set that he had was a leaded. I can remember the latest set that he had was a leaded. Now, the set right before the leaded was a collapsible set that he had. He got that when he had gone to New York in 23 with the Pierron's band. It was the folding bass drum. When it would collapse, you could handle it just like any other suitcase.
I can't imagine exactly how it is. People have tried to describe it to me. We've got some descriptions of it. The way it was made, honestly, when it would fold, it was the two head.
It would be in a circle and a half circle. Then it would form, that would be almost like a triangle, you could say.
Well, the head would fold up? Yeah, the head would fold.
Oh, I didn't know that.
Yeah, the head would fold.
See the head and the shell.
Was the shell metal or wood? Metal. Metal.
It was metal and with hinges, too.
Do you think you could show us better? Would it be clearer if I brought a bass drum over? There's one across the street.

Well, I guess I could. Now, the other father that I've seen, it's only two that I've ever seen. My father with one at Sonny Greer of the Duke Ellings Band, he had one. Sonny Greer had one. He had one when they were on tour and when they were playing theaters and they would play dances on outside. With Ellington. With Ellington. He had a collapsible drum. He had a collapsible bass drum.
Did it have regular rods? You know, did you tighten up things? Yes, I did have regular rods when it was set up. Once you got it set up, then you tighten up the rods.
Yeah, you tighten the rods, yeah, for both sides. That's right. Regular skin heads. Regular skin head.
Yeah.
Difficult to visualize it.
Yeah, how that shell could fold up, but I guess they had something worked out.
Yeah, well, it was with hinges, you see.
You remember who made that? Nah. We might even find an old catalog with it illustrated something. That's possible. It came to New York and all of that. Yeah, it came from New York where he got it.
I can't remember the name. I really couldn't remember the name.

Do you remember, did he ever say, or do you remember personally, what kind of sticks he used if they were heavy or lightweight or longer than usual or what kind of? They were just about number five, I think, in those times.
They were running by numbers. They weren't real heavy sticks.
They weren't real heavy sticks.
No, he never used real heavy sticks.
He used heavier ones on the street by any chance. No, the same sticks. He would use the same sticks each time. And on the street did he usually play the snare drum? Most of the time. I know.
Most of the time he used snare drum.
Did he use the same snare drum that he used in a dance orchestra?

Well, he did, but he had on the last, he was using a duplex out on the street. It was a duplex snare drum. I think Lester San Diego had one of the models of the one that he had. I think Lester has it now.
Can I believe Alfred Williams, doesn't that, a duplex? The one that boy from England here last year bought one from Alfred Williams. Yeah, I'm not sure. I think it was. I believe it is a duplex.

Because at the time it was only two in town. It was one that was of nickel and one of brass. And my father had both of them. The first one he had bought was the one with brass. And then he gave or traded that one over to a drummer during that period by the name of Wooligan. Now, I think his name was William Wooligan or Bill Wooligan. And he had the nickel one. And that was the only two that I've ever seen. And I do believe the one that San Diego had now is the one that my father had. Is he really? I believe that's the one.
When you say of nickel and of brass, you mean the rods on it or?
No, the shell.
Well, it wasn't a wooden shell.
Where the head was was wooden, but the shell was nickel. It was nickel and it was a brass shell and it was perforated.
Then the rim around up at the top was wood.
Was wood. That's correct. That's correct.
You say it's perforated?
Yeah, it was perforated. The shell was.
With holes in it?
Yeah, holes in it. Very light. Maybe, I mean, it really was a light drum. It's nothing like with the drum now because the snare drum now hit much heavier than what that was. Yeah.

Was it a very deep one, you know, say five or six things or seven or eight or? Just about five or six. Five or six rather. Just about. Shallower, medium. Just about what they use practically now. And he didn't use a deeper drum on the street?
No, no. Never did. It was just.
Can you tell us anything about his teaching of drums? Did you ever see any drum pupils come there and hear him give a voice of any of them? Oh, yes. What he did?

Oh, yes. He always started them off first, just as he did with me. He started them the same for his, for some. Then after it would be with the pad because he said it would develop a better wrist on a pad than to try him out on a drum. Oh, wow. Because he had exceptional wrist and I must say, by me and my father, I've never heard anyone roll a drum equally and as smooth as he had. Just about everybody's told us that ever mentioned when they talk about that role. And he believed in the wrist. Of course, it was from the way he was trained. Now, the way he was trained, my father came up with very poor parentage. And it was a friend of his that was getting music instruction. And they were inseparable at the time. It was a fellow by the name of John Kornfeld. It was a white father. You see, they came up boys together. And my father had the ambition of learning drums, but didn't have the sufficient funds to have anyone to teach him. So, just because of the friendship, as the boy would get his lesson, he would come back and he would teach it to him. Now, that's the training that my father got. He got his musical training. And he and John, I mean, they were inseparable up until death. Well, John died first. And my father always kept in contact with his family.
Did he ever amount to anything as a drummer? I mean, did he go ahead professionally?

Yeah, he was a good drummer too. He was a professional drummer. He played in several of the theaters and the orchestra was around. Good drummer. Yeah, he was a good drummer also. And that's the way he got his training. And there was one thing he always distressed was because of the wrist and the role. That was the most essential thing about playing the drums. You see, that's the way he was taught. And especially when he came down to playing timpanis, that would be the same thing.
Well, I think of it. Did your father live most of his life on that Robertson Street home? Or that he moved around?

Well, he moved in several spots. That was the spot where I was born. Prior to that, he was living on Dourmen Street right across from the Artesian Hall. That's where the three older children were born. And me and my younger sister, we were born on the Robertson Street address. Now, after we left the Robertson Street address, that's where we moved down on Ennett, where my father died down in that section. But originally, he came up right at La Harp and Claiborne, right across from where Muley is, a place of business is right now. He came up right in that section.
I think Louis DeLio, you know, big guy, Larry Nelson. All those folks. He was born on La Harp and raised right in that section.
Brown in that section. That's the section he came up.

I was going to ask, and I'm trying to get real personal, but about your home. Did your father have a special room for the teaching his music? Well, he always did. Yeah, it was always in the living room.
Did he have a piano? He did have a piano. Yeah.

He did have a piano because he, my sister's the oldest one. She didn't learn how to play. Well, you mentioned the three older children. Were they all a girl? All girls. All girls. In other words, it was five of them. I was the only boy. Yeah. And the oldest sister learned piano then? Yes. Did she ever play with any bands or any players?

No, never did play professionally. Just played in the home. My younger sister, she still plays in the school right now. Mostly classical music or what type of music? Classical. Mostly classical music and sheet music.
Yeah. Thank you. Do you remember how much your father charged for lessons?
Yes. At one time he was charging 25 cents and I think when he died, he was charging was 50 cents.
Of course, money was a little more valuable then than now, but still it was a low price for a famous teacher.

And the last student of his that really turned out to be a real nice drummer was Freddie Coleman. That's the last one. Coleman was his last student that I can remember. Now, another one that was his student, I was a very small boy at the time, it was Albert France. I don't know if you knew Albert France. Yeah, we interviewed him a couple of weeks ago. Albert was one of his students. Ernest Trepanyu was another one of his students. And so many of the boys were students. In fact, most of the drums in that period would come around. The older ones. They said they had a few lessons coming. Yeah, they would come around. That's right.

And if they didn't, I'm going to say quite a few of them, maybe like Baby Dodds even, who went to Chicago. I think he only had a few lessons. He wouldn't tell us too much about it. I think your father didn't get along too well with him. He didn't learn to read fast enough or something. Well, it could have been that. He was kind of impatient. I'll tell you that. That was one thing why I didn't want to learn how to play a drum. Because he was a little impatient. Even if they only took a few lessons, there's maybe sometimes none at all. They all tell about how they followed him in parades. Oh, yes, they did a lot of them. Followed him. They did admire him a lot.

Because you take a few of the old times that's still living, like, Happy Goldstein, he always remarked to me what a wonderful father my father was, and the way he used to admire walking behind him, second line, just to hear him play. And so many of the other boys. You take like the two minor boys, I can remember faintly them coming over to them. That was minor hall, I mean the two hall boys, and Baby Hall. In Tubby Hall, yeah. Tubby Hall, that's right. Yeah, Tubby Hall, I can remember.

I knew both of them quite well, one in Chicago and the other in Los Angeles. Yes. Both dead now. They are. Minor Hall just died about a year ago. Just about. Yeah, but just about everybody I ever talked to mentioned your father, I guess, from here. Any drummer and others too. Is there anything else you can tell us about his drum set? Well, I think that as far as cymbals or wood blocks or the hall bells, what else did he use?

He used all those. I can remember with orchestra bells, I can remember with the triangle, I can remember with the wood block, the crash cymbal. The other cymbal that they used to place on the bass drum, also with a spar. And they would hit the bass drum and the cymbal on the side for an effect at the time. Several different whistles that he would have. One, he would be working in theaters, because he'd work in theaters, going to the old lyrics in several of those theaters. Dolphin was running at the time.
Did he ever have one of those little ratchets, the little thing you'd turn?

That's right, on the side. Yeah, I have one of those. I think, I'm not sure. We may have one of those around the house. Knife, I'm not mistaken. One of those small things, ratchets. Yeah. Practically everything to go with drums at that period, he had it.

Did he ever use a slapstick? Yes, he had one of those too. Did he have one of those? And I know some drummers, of course, Chinese used to play the solos on the slide whistle. Louis Armstrong later had one of those. That's right, Louis. Did your father ever? My father had one of those too.
Just about everything. My father had one of those and at one time my father, he didn't do it often, then the other fellas had a way that he would take the snare drum and he would holler through it.
Oh, he did the holler? I've seen Chinese. Chinese does it, yeah. Showed his head once and Sammy Penn a little bit does it sometimes.
It gives Satan effect with the snare and the vibration that it would give.
Did he sing? He really sing or just sort of give a special like a break or something, a few little hollers or something?
It would be more on a type of a rhythm while the band would be playing and it's just another effect of a rhythm that would come out of it.
You say like he'd holler into it?
Yeah, they would be playing, you know, and it would be like an after beat or something with the snare drum. Where they would, I guess it's from the pressure.
When they put it right up against his face or whatever?
No, they would blow on it. Blow on it? Yeah, blow on it. Some effect against the snare and with the head, you see, and the effect of the snare on it, it would give a sound.
Not sure, that's not what Sammy Penn does in these acts. No, no. Sammy Penn sings.
He sings to it somewhere to make it rattle along with him. No, my father didn't sing. Would you think it might be the vibration of the lips like when you play a trumpet or something like that?
No, it wouldn't. It was more of a ha, ha, you see the vibration on the snare.

Yeah. Yeah, pretty good. Is there anything else unique, unusual that he did like that that you can think of? I hate to keep asking you so many questions, but you're the best chance that we'll ever have to learn anything about him.
One thing about him, especially on the street, he didn't have what most fellas would have, would be one of those belts around him. It was just a...
Yeah, the whole harness and all of them.

Yes, he wouldn't use any of those. All he would use was just an ordinary book strap. One of the book straps and the way he would balance his drum. He said it was much better that way from the way he wanted.
Around his shoulder, you mean?

Just across the shoulder. Just with one strap. A regular book strap in those days. Something like, you'll notice with the Army belt. One thing was one of those little narrow book straps that appeared. Yeah.

Yeah. See, and he would just... Yeah, that's amazing. Just fastened onto the drum probably at one place then. Yeah, that would go over his shoulder and the way he would hold it. Probably had a very light, as you mentioned, perforated and all very light. Yeah, it was light. It was light drum. It was light drum. Yeah. Is there anything else about his drumming style? You mentioned at first about the two beat rhythm and all that he developed. It was probably the first one, you say, in the dance bands at all.
Yeah, yeah. It's supposed to be. Of course, I can remember him in the dance band, but often heard that he was the first one to be used in the dance band.

Anything about his style of playing that you can say that is... Well, say compared to the drummers now. Of course, a lot of people think the drummers today are too noisy and jump all over the place, you know. Did he... Is he very active or was he a rather quiet drummer? Or what did you say?

Well, he was active, I think, for the period of time. I'll tell you someone that reminds me a lot of him now is Josiah Frazier. Oh, yeah. Yeah, it was more on that type. You see, just about the way Frazier plays, that was most of my father's style of playing. The way Frazier plays now.

Yeah, I was noticing Saeed the other week, he seems to hit the bass drum on one and three. One and three. That's right. That's the two beat. That's what they call the two beat. The one and three. And then his snares seem to more accent the two and four.
That's right. That's correct. Now, Begaard is another one of his... Pupil.
Yeah, Begaard coming around. Wow. He told us all about him too. He tried a bit about his lessons with him too. Usually, how often did he teach a pupil? One after... Twice a week. Twice a week.

Generally, it would be Tuesdays and Fridays. No, yeah, Tuesdays and Fridays and Wednesdays and Saturdays. Those were the four days that he would... Four days. They had different ones coming on those days.
Did he work almost every night that you can remember when you were young? When I was young or...

Well, that's all he ever did. Mostly every night he was working. Yeah, mostly every night he was working. And of course, what I can remember as a kid, the biggest layoff that I can remember is when they came back from New York. And 23 and 24 looked like when they came back. It was kind of rough at the time. But other than that, he was always going to go home.
And as I said, I'm not trying to get personal, but did he sleep pretty late then or... No, my father... Did he have another day job or what did he do?

No, all he did was just play the music. Now, he'd get up generally around about 9, 9.30 and then he was gone. Then he'd come back in the afternoon around about 4 or in the evening that he would teach, say about 3, 3.30 when the boys would be coming to school and then he would teach then. And get about an hour, sleep in the afternoon and then he'd be gone again. Because he was a fellow that had to go out every day.
Most of the jobs that he had, you remember if he had to take his drums almost every night to different places?
No, no. Most of the jobs was always appointment and job. He didn't have transportation. That's right.
Did he ever complain about it? Like you say, that influenced you in picking up there and that. Did he ever complain?
Yeah, especially when they had to get pointed. At that time it was a little dinky streetcar, something like the streetcar in Frisco, you know?
Oh yeah, there was a little thing that they had to turn on, chain or something. Yeah, that's right. Cable car.

Cable car. The only thing that was run by electricity down here. And they had to get an appointment and they wouldn't be allowed at a certain time on the streetcars with the instrument. He would always manage whenever he had to go someplace or play at night, he would get there in a day. Because I think it was between four and eight that they weren't allowed and from six to nine, so he would go in there and set up his instrument for that night. And there was only certain hours they were allowed to take the drums? Drums on the streetcars. That was the only means of transportation they mostly had during that period.
Yeah. And nobody had a car in those days? No. And you had to have a permit even for those hours? Yes, for drums and those bass bombers. They had to have an appointment.
They had to have a permit.
Well this to me suggests that there must have been a lot of drummers and bass players going on streetcars. They did.

If they weren't going on streetcars they would be walking. You take so many of the guys that walk from one engagement to another from their home. I heard Boca stayed on the session down at the Jean-Sami Hall, that drummer that he played with during that period was a fellow by the name of Veen. And Veen walked all the way up to the protection and I went back with his drum.

One funny story, I remember Natty Dominic, you know Don Albers of course. Yes, I know Natty too. His uncle, Natty Brave on Chicago. We got about six or seven tapes, the story of his life. Talked to him a long time and he started out on drums, I'm pretty sure. Maybe he had a few lessons with your father. Yeah, I know he talked about your father.
I wouldn't be surprised because they were very good friends.

Only a short time because on about his first job, I think it was a job with Buddy Petit, he said way up at Louisiana Avenue, so he was going to walk up there. He got up along where the pawn shops are on Ramport, took his drums in there and pawned them and went back home. Went back home. Didn't show up for the job. His father gave him a hard whipping that night and all and then later he went to Emmanuel Perez and took up the trumpet, the carnet. But that's the way he did on his first job, gave him up right there, stopped and pawned them. They were good neighbors too because they lived right across from each other, Perez and down on 8 Quartz Street.
Because that's where I can recall them very well.
Oh, another thing here, I'm just getting ready to fill in your name here on the first tape box. We're about out of it. And how is that spelled, the last name, the Cottrell? How do you spell it?

C-O-T-R-E-L-L, that's the way we register. Two L's. That's right. And truthfully, the name is really C-O-T-R-E-L-L-E. My father dropped it somewhere and that's the way we all registered. It used to be Cottrell, the way they would pronounce it.
It would be Cottrell, C-O-T-R-E-L-L-E. You must have heard a lot of people around here call it Contrell. Contrell, Cantrell.
Yeah. So many things, but it's Cottrell.
Yeah. I just wondered how that got started. I looked up in the city directories, I noticed there must have been an Italian name of, oh, maybe a couple of dozen of Contrell, C-A-N-T-R.
Yeah.
And probably a lot of people knew maybe an Italian name, but have you had any explanation for the reason they call it that?

All I can see is because of that French section down in town, plenty of them would call him Contrell, Cottrell from the accent, but how it got started, I couldn't say. In your father's time, did they call him that too? They called him Contrell, they called him Cantrell, some would call him Catrell. Right through his face.
They didn't know the difference.
Yeah. But most of the old ones called him Cottrell. Cottrell.
Uh-huh.
It's sort of a French form.
French, it is. Yeah. I don't know if it's, I guess, Cantrell looked almost like it was an Italian name, but I guess the first names, I'm not sure.
Mm-hmm.
So I always wondered how that got started, and I never knew for sure for years. No, I don't know. Because a lot of them call me the same thing then.
They'll say Contrell or Cantrell, Cantrell. Yeah. But Peter Bocais and the father's name, they always called him Cottrell.
Do you know anything about your father's ancestry if they came from France? Yes. Or the French family? Yes, his father didn't come from France.

His father came from France. There was two brothers, which would be my grandfather and my granduncle. They both were from France. His mother came from up in St. John, St. Jane, one of those. Yeah, that's where she came from. And that's as far as I can remember from that end. His mother's name was Miriam Bernard, and his father's name mentioned in the same Louis Albert Cottrell. He's just going on the line, just carrying it through.
Your father's name was exactly the same as my dad.
In other words, I'm the third.
Oh, I see.
But they called Junior, you know, after the grandfather died, they began calling me Junior. And we just did.

This feels about over. There's another minute or two, if there's anything else we can think of about your father and we're getting into your life. For instance, do you know how old he was when this other boy began helping him with the drums?
Yeah, just about 11, 12 years old.
Just around that period.
It was quite real.
And did he ever tell you about his first jobs or the first bands he played with? You mentioned Robichaux for one.

Robichaux is one of the bands that I do remember him speaking of as an orchestra. But you take way back was the old Excelsa band, which was not of the group in later years. I think it was the original band was Tio and Dublé band. And then it went into the name of Excelsa band. Was that Brass Band mostly?
That's Brass Band.
Oh, it was Brass Band. Of course, the Brass Band in that area, they would play for outdoor parties and everything else during that time. That's what I've heard they play for dancing even.
They would. They would.

That was a man made up of I think some of Mineta's relatives, some of his older group. Some names that I don't even remember. Another name that I can't recall of was Crusto. He was a trumpet player. I think he was the one that had taught Perez if I'm not mistaken. Crusto and then there's a fellow by the name of Boasso. He was the old baritone in the area. I also worked with the old, well they were about in the same area. Like Vic Gasper and his brother. Yes. Old Gasper. George Fields. He was, I think he's dead just about five or six years now.
Maybe.

No, no. Another father he played with was Charles Elgar. I knew him. He's still up there. He's an officer in the union. He's vice president. He's vice president. Many years. They were just about the same age. My father might be one or two years older than he. A fellow by the name of Ralph Marniegu. That was another one in that old brass band in that area. Ralph Marniegu. That was a soldier. Who I saw. I heard him mention out. I said Crusto. That's the name. Diddy Chandler. Diddy Chandler came up right around in the same area. With my father. I'll often know him speak of me and Mac Murray.

Oh yes. We never didn't know much about Mac Murray. You happen to know what his real name... Some people say his first name was Mac and his last name Murray? No, that was his last name. His last name was Mac Murray. Now, I'm trying to think what was his first name.

I can't recall, but that was his last name. Paul Barber and maybe thought his name was John Mac Murray. I think it was John Mac Murray. I'm not sure. I'm not sure, but Mac Murray was his... Was his whole name when big names. Yeah, it was his last name.
Do you remember anything about John Veen? Oh, yes. I can remember John Veen. His son is up now.
I don't know. The lady was over there, the sort of superintendent of the hall. Of the building. That's Jean Vigne's daughter. Oh, I didn't know.
Yeah, that's his daughter. The Jeannemie Hall. The Jeannemie Hall, yeah.
At the time you made the record, then we got to see her. Yes.
But let us in the back door or something. Yeah, she's still there, right? No.
The one that prepared the sandwiches and things.
Oh, yeah? Yeah, well, that's his daughter. That's Jean Vigne's daughter. She probably know a good deal about it.
Oh, yeah, I'm sure she can. Get plenty of it.
Yeah.

Yeah, I can remember him. I was just where the Iberville Project is now, which was part of Storyville at the time. Well, he used to run a wooden cold yard, and he, and I know my daddy, and then they would have rehearsals sometime in the back of the cold yard some days when business would be slow and the guys would meet around there. And I can remember him from that area, going there, listening to them rehearsal. I was just about seven, six years old around the time I can recall. Very interesting. Yeah, Jean Vigne, Mike Murray, D.D. Chandler, and my father, all of it was around the same period, and I guess just about on the same type. Uh-huh. Because those were the ones that I often heard it mention about. Also, this other fellow, well he strictly played just bass drum and a brass band was Giles. Now what's Giles' first name? I can't remember.
Yeah, I can't remember now. Wait a minute.

I don't know. But was the uncle's name? I don't know. I don't know if it was relative or not. But I know his name was Giles. That was the last funeral that my father played, because Giles' funeral was just about a month or a month and a half before my father.
Your father was active right up to the end?
Oh yeah, he was active until the day before he-
Oh really?

Sudden death. Sudden death. It was a heart attack, yeah. He had worked at night up on the roof garden, there was a Peron band there. He was running the place at the time. And up until it was just about 11.30, they were getting ready for a break, because he spoke to me and he said, I want you to get home. You know, you have to start school early in the morning. So I said, okay. When I got home, I just did beat him home, to be true, for about maybe about 10 or 15 minutes, because when I heard the door, he was coming in. I jumped in bed and I had clothes and everything, just with shoes on, because I didn't want him to know that I had just gotten in. And about 20 minutes after he was in, we just heard a sound when we got to him. He was just smothering when we got to him. He was just passing out. He just was on the hall of time. He'd wake up until the time that he died.

I was going to ask about Walter Brundy, another drummer. Walter Brundy was another one. I just faintly remember. That was another one of my father's scholars. He studied his and he never got to know Walter at all. He used to talk a lot about Walter. Yeah, well I met Walter just a little before
he died. Well he was playing saxophone and he was out in Texas at the time. I think he was just a
clarinet and sax. I think he was killed in an auto accident. That's right.

Run over or something. Those were, I can remember a picture with Brundy, instead of having the rods tuned where it was with the rope. And the ropes, the little ears, some people got a little leather ears. That's right. That's what they used to in the bass drum.
Remember, did your father ever use one of those? I can't remember him with those. Probably had the most modern equipment. He did. I must say, he always kept the most modern
equipment. Anything came out new, he always had it. Before we leave him, as I said, I don't like to keep

pumping more information about your father, but it's a wonderful opportunity for us to hear about him from the best possible source. Anything else about the bands he played with? Anything about the Pierron band in particular, the trip to New York? Did you remember? Oh yes, I can remember. When he first,

that I can recall that he remember, when he first left New Orleans in 1917, he left with Manuel Perez's band and they went to Chicago. I think it was at, I think Mike Fritz was the proprietor's name that they worked up there for. That was before Joe Oliver and them had gone up there. That was in 1917. And then that man was Perez, Lorenzo Teo, my father, Eddie Atkins, and Frankie Haney was playing piano. Well, he stayed there for about nine months and then he came and made a visit home on a vacation for two weeks and he went back. He came back in 1918. 1919, he went back again. He came back in 20. That was Manuel Perez again? Yeah, that was with Manuel Perez. Because Manuel stayed up there the whole time through. But my father, you know, he went and then came back. Then in 20 he came and he stayed and he went with John Robichaud again in the 20s. That's when they were working in the Lyric and he stayed there for about a year. Then he joined Pierron's band. They were working on the Spanish Foda at the time. And he stayed with the Pierron's band until the time of his death. In 1923, that's when they had gone up to New York. They worked at the Roseland and Ballroom and I think it was Cotton Club too. I don't know if it was
Did he ever say how the band was received up there? Write letters back or anything?

He wrote and said the band was, well, it was a different style playing all together than what they were playing up there because they were alternating in the Roseland Ballroom at the time. That was when Fletcher Henderson was just beginning to get prominent back then in 23. And it was a dancing school. In other words, it was a taxi dance that Roseland Ballroom was at that time and they were alternating with the Fletcher Henderson band. And of course there was two different styles of playing all together, different type of music because Fletcher was born at Eastern style at the time and what they had. See the band was received pretty well but it was one of those things like you were looking for that pot of gold at the end of that rainbow and it looked like it never happened. They came back and the popularity was increasing down in here again. They made one or

two more recordings and they went back in 24. Oh yes, have you ever heard those recordings? We just picked up one of them last week, the Red Man Blues written by Peter Boccage. I was just asking Ralph, that's the last

one that I can recall that they made down here. It had Teal almost all the way through. I think it did. Yeah. And that was the record that was made down here, I think I was in 25 when they made that down

in here, that Red Man Blues. You of course have heard them. I just wondered if you're familiar enough with them. Can you compare that to the way the band really sounded in person? Did it sound as good as the band? Of course no records ever sound I guess as good as the real thing but you know. Well to be truthful,
which has been so long since I wasn't wanting to record that I can't remember. I couldn't remember
as of now. I just took that up to Tulane last week, I wish I'd kept it here. We could have played that for you.

I really couldn't remember but in that time, P-Ron had really what you would call a society band. It had a nice punch and majority of the musicians always did look up to P-Ron's band as being more of a cultured band. Yes, I know.

I know. You can tell some of that on the records too. Well with the violins, the featuring of the violin and everything too. It was more of a smooth, sweet band I guess. That's right. T.O. comes through quite a bit on some of those things too but otherwise you can't always tell so much about T.O.'s tone and all. I guess we might as well get on with your life now a little bit more. Maybe you can tell us a little bit more about T.O. too since he's also gone. Yeah, well. Just what style he played and how his tone was and style and you know. Well now if I was to be frank with you,

other than the recording, I didn't hear T.O. too much as a player. Bare little I mean that I could make any comparison as whether to like or not to like. It's funny, Omer Simeon, you know, who was a great

player in New York and also studied with T.O. Yeah. And up in Chicago, he says the same thing. He was so young he wasn't allowed to go around the dance halls. Well that's right. So you never really heard him play much. He can't remember much whether he used Albert or Bing's system, aren't he? Well I knew he used Albert. I can readily remember that. Well I think he knew that much but I mean he couldn't remember much about his instrument or how he played or sounded because he just took lessons and that was about all.

And speaking of Simeon, T.O. used to tell me all the time when I was taking lessons from him, he always rated Simeon as his best scholar. He did, huh? He did. He said for one reason, Simeon had that initiative and that determination to really learn and he said that's the only scholar that he ever had that he didn't have to send back the second time on the lesson. Yeah. Yeah. He said Simeon was just, just that way. And he said each time he came he was ready. There's no saying,
well come back, you don't know it that well this time. Uh-huh. That's about, what year now did you study with him? Let's see, you were born 1911.
I was born in 1911. I began studying with T.O. in 1922.
22? Yeah. Quite young. And you say that first you had the soft edge. Yes. How long did he keep you on soft edge? Well that was your father. My father had me on soft edge. Oh, but did T.O. also?

No, T.O. didn't because when I went there, well he wanted to see just how advanced I was. Well after going over and knowing some of the rudiments and division, he said that I was ready for the instrument. And he placed me on the instrument. And then he loaned you a C clarinet? C clarinet. Yes, he did. It was a C clarinet. Even the C was a little large for me. And his C flat planted, well he was using it quite regularly then, so he wouldn't let me in. So he said,
well use this. It's been wonderful. It didn't play that alone. But you say he used his C flat, what did he use it on parades?

Parades and funerals. Yeah, because he played brass band around here until he was paralyzed. I didn't know about that. Yeah, he took with a stroke in 1925, laid him up for about six months. Then he was able to play again, but he wasn't able to march on the street. Well I never knew that. We interviewed his brother and every,
a lot of people that had studied with him, but nobody ever told us to him before.

Yeah, 25. He got, he became stricken with paralysis. He was playing a funeral one evening. And it began on him. And that night after he got on the job, he worked a while and they had to bring him home.
Yeah, it's terrible.
No, Jake, I don't know if you've ever met Adolph Alexander. Oh yes, Tats? Yeah, Tats. That's another one of these ex-students too.
Oh, that's right.

And Tats always remarked now that he knew just what it was after Lorenzo had gotten paralyzed, because something about his fingers, he cannot execute on his clandest like he had once did before. He said he knew what Lorenzo was saying when he said, well, that was it as far as playing like he used to, because he never could regain that form that he had. That was after the New York trip then? That was after the New York trip. That was in 25. Did he die up in New York though? He went back to New York. He stayed here until about 1930, the latter part of the 30s. Then he went to New York and he died while he was in New York. I think it was either 30 or 31 when he died in New York.

I knew his wife, I think his wife just died two or three years ago. Just about, just about. That's right. That's why I thought he died there too. Yeah, he did die over there. Did he go back to play on that trip? Can you remember?

Yeah, he went back. He was playing while he was up there, because I think he was with Jelly Roll at the time, or Woken in and out around at the time of his death. Because that's what he had gone back up there. Depression had set in after 29 and things that were going to get very slow and money was hard to get. Oh yeah, that's right. Depression was on there. So he went and he went by boat up there, because that was the cheaper way of transportation. He got up there. Now it's either 32 or 33. I don't recall exactly the year that he died. I think maybe his brother might have told us. Yeah, but it's long in that period that he died.

I was going to ask, it reminds me in New York, I heard years ago of rumors that he had sold some numbers to Ellington, like maybe he'd helped write Mood Indigo, you know, that slow blues type thing. And Barney Bigard once told me, I remember about the last time I saw Barney, when he was back with Louie at the time before the present time, in Chicago. And he said that T.O. had sold him several tunes, he thought. He'd written some of those things. Do you know of any of his composing activities or anything that he ever wrote? Or did your father ever write?

Directly I don't, but I do recall on several times going for lessons, where he would be writing and he used to say that if this ever would go over, what it would mean to him. He said, this is something that I'm composing about. What it is, or how many it is, I don't know. At least you know he was active. Yeah, I know he was active to that extent. You know, speaking of T.O., so many days that I would go there and I would be disappointed because he did drink a lot and he would be drunk. And he said, well I'm sorry, I just can't give you no less today, come back next time, you know, next trip,
one of those things. I don't think anybody ever mentioned, not that we're, we try to specialize in

the way it is. Well no, I mean it's just the way it is. Yeah, it's just facts, it's just the way it was. That was the thing with his claim, where when he had gone back to New York and he had begun drinking again, and after he was told that it was detrimental to him and he would continue that it was short in his life. So his wife had told me, well there's nothing she could do, that's just the way he took it. Yeah, well it's hard to say. And then when he met up with Bayshade up there again, that was it. Because several days she wouldn't see him when she would call to find out he was somewhere with Bayshade.

Yeah, it's hard to say. I think about Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds. I guess you didn't know the Dodds brothers, do you remember them? I don't remember them. I knew of them after they left. I knew them both in Chicago. Johnny never took a drink in his life hardly and Baby was quite a drinker. Yeah. Johnny died when he was 48 and Baby kept drinking and drinking and the other he lived to be 65 or so. That's right. Doesn't usually really kill him, but it might make it a little worse if they have that stroke. Maybe he had that trouble too, but he kept on. Johnny died from sort of a stroke then, weren't you? Johnny died of a stroke. Oh, speaking of the T.O.'s, do you remember the older men, either the old Lorenzo or the Papa? I remember the uncle for Papa very well. I don't remember Lorenzo's daddy. Lorenzo Senior, but I do remember. I think he was, I think it was the old man. Is it Louie T.O.? Louie T.O. That's his name. The brother that's still living. Yeah. Said that their father went back, I believe, to over on the Gulf Coast, either Biloxi or something. Bay St. Louis. That's where they were. You remember the uncle then? Oh, I remember the uncle very well. How did he compare with, in playing with the young Lorenzo? Well, if you can remember well enough to the sound, I know it's... The sound, I think the sound was about the same. And

the old man was more of a, like we would use the term, was more of a softer player than Lorenzo. Lorenzo was more forceful. But the sound was almost the same. I don't think it just wasn't that much in
volume, you see? And you remember in your childhood, the youngest, very youngest, remembrance is that the old man was still teaching that his papa was... Yeah, I can remember because

he died in 22. He died in 22. I can remember very well when he died. He used to visit home quite often. He and his wife both. He was a friend of your father. Yeah, he was. Because the father was most old as a son or something under him, you see. And he's... And at one time, they were neighbors too. And Mrs. Teal and the old man, they used to visit home often. And I can remember them on the street, but like I said before, I used to remember the playing and the style. I can't... I really can't remember his playing.

I remember once, speaking of Natty Dominic again, he said he remembers when he was a little boy, once Papa Teal heard a jazz band like out on a wagon or something and came running in their house and wanted to hide under the bed or something. That noise is a disgrace to music. It's a disgrace to New Orleans. He didn't really like jazz. He liked classical music. He did. Yeah, I guess so. I think even symphonic work he did his time and conducted that group and everything else.
Speaking on this, we were saying a few minutes ago, we were talking about the band at the Tuxedo and the dance club. Yeah, the Tuxedo was organized in the year of 1910.

I don't remember the exact month or date, but I did get that information from the picture, which William Ridgely, maybe Ridgely had died not so long ago, he had of the Tuxedo band. And that original Tuxedo band, it was Ridgely on trombone, Celestine on trumpet. My father was playing drum, the Razzatea was playing clarinet, Peter Boccage was playing violin. And it was at the Tuxedo club, somewhere down in Stewartville or the old district. Frankman Street. Somewhere along there. That was the first Tuxedo band. And they were replaced afterwards, well Ridgely and Celestine continued. And the next one to come in the band, because that was the second picture, I remember was Jimmy Noon. He was a clarinetist in that band. Then they had, uh, Winnie Strapani was the drummer in the band. I think they discarded the violin, instead of the violin they had the ghetto, which was Willie Bontag. I don't know if you ever remember. I met him one.
You met him? Oh yeah. Is he still living? Oh no. No, he's dead now.

Well it was Willie Bontag. I can remember that picture just as well in Ridgely's home as if I'm looking at it right now. And you say that's where the name, the Tuxedo. That's where it originated, from the club. And Ridgely and, uh, Solid Stanley kept that name going. It was originally Tuxedo

band until they had this. Well by the way, um, speaking of Willie Bontag, I can't pronounce those French names, but Zutty, I used to know him quite well in New York. That's his nephew. And he used to tell me about his uncle, and so when I ran across him on the parade, I recognized the name as soon as I was introduced to the course. Didn't get to talk to him in a half a minute, of course. In those days I didn't, wasn't studying the history as much as I am now. Yeah, nah, yeah. But I was thinking about Zutty. Did he ever study with your father? Do you remember anything about him? I can remember Zutty, but as for taking this night, I don't remember. No, I don't recall. Um, or you mentioned Jimmy Newton. Do you remember much about him here? I don't. Have you ever heard him or anything?

Oh, I remember seeing pictures of Jimmy and hearing recordings of Jimmy. And I did meet Jimmy in Chicago, although that was back in 1937. But other than that, I didn't know too much other than what I hear.

You don't know where he learned, who he studied? No, I don't. I really don't. Because the reason why I ask is that he seems to have something in common with your style and Omosimeon's style. I wondered if he was a T.O. student too.

I couldn't say. I really don't know. I talked to him a little bit when we wrote the book Jazzman, which is pretty much out of date, but we didn't have any tape recorders to remember what they said. I'd have a few notes on it when I talked in 1938. He was a wonderful clarinetist. Yes, he was. He really was.
During that period, it was great. He didn't mention then.
He might have told me. Maybe I can look up my notes. I really could say.
One that's still around that may could give a little more information on that is a Wilmina Bordette. Do you know that?
I met her once and Lizzie Miles introduced me to her as her teacher or something from backstage of the Mardi Gras about five or six years ago, a long time ago. Yeah. I've never seen her since.
Because she always speaks of Jimmy Newland and the time that they were playing. Really? It looked like she worked with Jimmy for quite some time. You know, now I'm here.
I must try to see a reminder.
Is she in town?
I think she's across the lake.

Sometimes she's alternating between here and across the lake. You can reach her or her whereabouts. I think it's 168 or 1610 in that street. They can tell you just about 8 or 10. 8 or 10. 168 or 10. Somewhere along there. And that. And it. And they can tell you just about how to contact Wilmina. That'd be nice.

Yeah, Bunk used to talk about it too. I knew Bunk by the way. Yeah. Used to be a pianist at some of those Sunday concerts, as they called them, and they used to give. Barth. Barth. B-A-R-T-H-E-N. T-H-E-N. T-H-E-N. Oh, B-A-R-T. It may be B-A-R-T. Anyway, they'll never talk about it.
It's Wilhelmina Barth Duroon. That's her name. D-U. Yeah. That's right. I remember there is another name. D-U. Oh.
That's right. I remember there is another name.
Duroon? How would you spell it? I think capital D-U, capital R-U-E-N, the way it's spelled.

She's the one who used to always be sending cards into Tony Amarico, asking for Lizzie Miles. I think she is. Yeah. We'd give her full name sometime. I'd wonder if that's Wilhelmina Barth that I heard about. She played with Jimmy Noon.
Yeah. She used to always speak of Jimmy Noon, you know, in the days when she was playing. Wilhelmina played with so many during that period and played with so many of those that still play now.
I guess so.
Mm-hmm.

Are you watching the time, by the way? Do you have anything else that you have to run along to? We don't want to keep you doing this. No, I was just noticing. No, it's all right. Ralph arranged the interview and I didn't know just how long you had. No. I mean, he happened to see you. Really, really?

I saw Ralph over here when I worked that night and I came that Friday, but no one was here. Dick happened to be here. That's right. And no one was here. You had gone out. Dick was here a while. That's true. And so today when he came, well, I do know on Fridays is the only day that I do have a little time. That's true. So when I saw him there, I said, well, it's best today. I don't know when I'll have this time again. That's wonderful. We've been wanting to talk to him for a couple of years or so. Yes, I did. I made connections. And it seems as if I was the one that was always evading. I would tell you all right. Well, I know. You're just a busy man. That's right. That's right. You know the type of business that I'm in now. If you don't get out there and hustle, because I work on commission, you know how it is.

Sure. Yeah, that's right. You know how commission, brother. That's right. And with your musical activities, and the officer, the president of the union is naturally one of the busiest men I can imagine. Yeah. Thank you. Let's see if we have a few more minutes. Well, can we go back to, we were talking about the C clarinet.
Oh, the C clarinet. Well, the C clarinet. Yeah, for real. Well, I kept the C clarinet.

He kept me on the C clarinet for about six months. And after six months, he said, well I think from practicing and all that, your fingers make it stretch to the B flat. Well, that's when I got my B flat clarinet.
Now, did he say anything about your mouthpiece or your reeds? For instance, do you put your teeth on the upper part of the mouthpiece or do you use just your lips on there?
Well, the way I was trained, he had to hold my lip kind of tight on the bottom with the teeth done.
Cover it.
Yeah. Teeth covered on the bottom? Yeah. Against the reed.

The lip. No. The lip covering the teeth. Uh-huh. And the upper teeth on the mouthpiece. The upper teeth on the mouthpiece. On the mouthpiece. Oh. He said, now, of course, that's the way I was taught. He said, but those kind of things, they vary. It depends on the individual sometimes. He said, you may take it and always have a bite like that and it may come a time when you don't want a bite. So, truthfully speaking, you notice I don't have the malk like most of them have. Yeah. I probably say, well, but it kind of worried me a while. Uh-huh. And you take, they have a lot of clarinets that they- Clared down. They're wearing it out. Because Teo's was partly worn himself, you see. And he did have the bite, but I never did really get myself accustomed to really biting with my upper teeth.
No. That's what I thought when I watched you play, you seemed to have more pressure with your lip.

Yeah. That's right. I never did. Because he told me that's the way he was taught. He thought that was the proper way. He said, but you can't go by those things because he said, there's so many others that can get so much out of instruments and they violate rules and regulations. So he said, whatever way you can get the best result and the way it sounded to me, I'll let it go at that. Uh-huh.
What about the reed? Did you use a hard reed or a soft reed or-

Well, in the beginning I used a very soft reed. But then it was too reedy, he claimed. It wasn't getting the sound that he thought would be best. Uh-huh. So he told me to use a little stiffer reed. And then it depended on the way my amateur came. Now sometimes I can use a much stiffer reed and other times I'll have to switch to a soft reed. It depends just the way my mouth is.
What kind of teal used himself did he ever say? Mostly it was just about a medium hard.
Uh-huh.
It was a medium hard reed that he used. That would be about a number three nowadays, wouldn't it? Yeah, so. Uh-huh. Because in those days they weren't numbered anyway. That's right. I can say.

They would either shave or cut them down the way they felt was best. Do you remember anything about his instrument? How many keys he had on it? He had a 13. 13? The 13 clarinet. I can remember that. Remember the make by any chance? Buffet.

Yeah, it was a Buffet. I can remember it being a Buffet. The C clarinet that you had, do you remember the make of that? No, I really don't remember the make of that. Was that the regular 15 key? No, I think it was the 13 key. 13 key. Yeah, the 13 key. Mm-hmm. Yeah, it was 13 key. The loan did Lorenzo do? Yeah, it was his. It was his. Now, when you, you say you were on that about six months, when you went to the B flat, was that also unloaned from him? No.
He told my dad there was no need to push him because he knew that it wasn't going to be too long, you see. He said, my daddy bought me one. Uh-huh. It wasn't make of that.
It's the one that I have now.
Is that the same one? It's the same clarinet.
Wait a minute, that's a pencil mark? That's a mark. Yeah, I remember saying it with that. Yeah, it's the same clarinet. Mm-hmm. Wow, that's really held up a long time. It really did.
Uh-huh.
And what about the mouthpiece? Did you do anything to the mouthpiece or did you just have the same mouthpiece?

Well, the mouthpiece that I'm using now is a mouthpiece that was given to me by Bonnie Begaard. Oh, yeah. Yes, Begaard gave me that mouthpiece back in 33, but before then it was the same regular stout

mouthpiece from the horn that I had used. And do you find any difference in the tone between the two mouthpieces? Well, yes, I did. That's why I began using it. It made it a little broader because it was more of an open layer. But about the same kind of reed you've always used? Just a little softer reed. That's a soft. Now than what I had been using before.

I was using a much harder reed because the mouthpiece was a little closer. But the mouthpiece that was given to me by Begaard, by the layer being a little open, it made I use a softer reed. You know Begaard, when my father and I had gone to New York, well he taught me also. Oh yeah? Yeah. Because after they had gone and Lorenzo said he didn't want me to just be idling around and taking things on myself. So he had the choice of either sending me to Adolf Alexander or Begaard. So he said, well I think I'd rather send you to Begaard. Now at the time that he sent me to Begaard, Begaard wasn't playing clarinet at all. He had stopped playing clarinet. In other words, around here they wouldn't even employ him as a clarinet. They thought that he had played so bad. But Lorenzo said he thought that he would be the better instructor for me. He would be the better instructor for me. And I stayed with him until they came back. And Begaard didn't pick up these clarinet, he told me until around 1925 or 1926 somewhere when with the Olives and Van Olives. We were in Chicago. I thought that he really worked on it. What's the matter? You got that thing up there for you? Why don't you try and clear the thing? And he said it looked like they gave him an admission. And then he began studying hard on it again.
Was there any particular thing that Lorenzo would teach you? For instance, would he teach you anything about tapping your foot? Yes.

He did teach how to keep in time. He said, of course, as time go along, he wanted us to count with our footmen that he would teach us. That was to keep us right there that we wouldn't vary. He said, but then we must remember after we reached a certain stage and if we ever got to where we were playing professional music that that thing would stop. We must memorize those kind of things, or just have that feel for it.

And more or less keep time in your head. That's right. Well I know when I go to Mineta he teach me with my foot to tap on one and lift it up on two, down on three, and up on four. Well yes, that's the method that they taught, but Lorenzo didn't teach me that method.
Those that was taking lessons with him during that time, it was down on one, left on two, right on three, and up on four. That's the way he taught us. One, two, three. One, two, three.

segments.title: Opening, birth and father's death in 1927
segments.summary: Russell opens the session; Cottrell gives his name, 1911 birth on Robertson Street, and his father's death in 1927 when he was 16.

segments.title: Starting clarinet: solfege with his father, then Lorenzo Tio Jr.
segments.summary: His father taught solfege first, Manuel Perez was his godfather, and he began clarinet on a C clarinet with young Lorenzo Tio.

segments.title: His father's appearance and why he was called Old Man Cottrell
segments.summary: Description of the father's height and build; he turned gray after returning from Chicago in 1917.

segments.title: Father as first New Orleans trap drummer and Wurlitzer salesman
segments.summary: He is credited with two-beat drumming and being first to use drums in orchestras (Robichaux); he adopted new equipment and sold instruments for Wurlitzer.

segments.title: The collapsible bass drum from New York
segments.summary: The folding two-head metal bass drum his father got in New York in 1923; Sonny Greer had one too.

segments.title: Father's sticks and perforated duplex snare drum
segments.summary: Light number-five sticks, snare on the street, and the nickel and brass perforated duplex snares, one now owned by Lester.

segments.title: How his father learned drums from John Kornfeld and taught the wrist roll
segments.summary: The father taught himself via a white boyhood friend's lessons and stressed wrist and the roll.

segments.title: Family homes and the music room
segments.summary: Where the family lived, the piano in the living room, and his four sisters.

segments.title: Lesson fees and his father's drum pupils
segments.summary: Lessons cost 25 to 50 cents; pupils included Freddie Coleman, Albert France, Trepagnier; many drummers followed his parades.

segments.title: Father's percussion effects, slapstick and snare 'holler'
segments.summary: He used bells, wood block, cymbals, whistles, ratchet and slapstick, and an effect of blowing on the snare.

segments.title: Father's shoulder strap and drumming style
segments.summary: He used a plain book strap, and his style resembles Josiah Frazier's two-beat bass drum.

segments.title: Father's teaching schedule and daily routine
segments.summary: Pupils came four days a week; he played nearly every night and taught afternoons.

segments.title: Carrying drums by streetcar and on foot
segments.summary: Drums needed permits and set hours on streetcars; others walked to jobs.

segments.title: Story of Natty Dominique pawning his drums
segments.summary: Russell tells how Natty Dominique pawned his drums on his first job and then took up cornet with Perez.

segments.title: Spelling and pronunciation of the Cottrell name
segments.summary: The name is spelled Cottrell, once Cottrelle, often mispronounced Contrell or Cantrell.

segments.title: Father's French ancestry and being the third Louis Albert
segments.summary: Grandfather came from France; Cottrell is the third of the name, called Junior.

segments.title: Father's early bands: Excelsior brass band and Robichaux, with associates
segments.summary: His father's start at 11 or 12, the old brass band, and Crusto, Boasso, Gaspard, Fields, Elgar, Chandler and Mac Murray.

segments.title: Jean Vigne, his hall, and bass drummer Giles
segments.summary: Vigne's daughter and the coal yard rehearsals in Storyville; Giles's funeral was the last one his father played.

segments.title: His father's sudden death
segments.summary: His father worked on the roof garden with the Piron band, then died of a heart attack that night.

segments.title: Drummer Walter Brundy and his father's modern equipment
segments.summary: Brundy was a pupil later a sax player killed in a car accident; the father always had the newest gear.

segments.title: His father's travels: Chicago with Perez, Robichaux, then Piron
segments.summary: The 1917 Chicago trip with Manuel Perez, return to Robichaux, then Piron's band until 1927.

segments.title: The Piron band in New York and its recordings
segments.summary: The Piron band alternated with Fletcher Henderson at Roseland in 1923; a society band, with the Red Man Blues record.

segments.title: Tio as a player and teacher; Omer Simeon his best pupil
segments.summary: Cottrell rarely heard Tio play; Tio rated Simeon his best scholar. Cottrell began lessons in 1922.

segments.title: Tio's loan of a C clarinet
segments.summary: Tio tested his progress and lent a C clarinet, since his own C-flat was in use for parades.

segments.title: Tio's stroke, decline and death in New York
segments.summary: Tio was paralysed in 1925, could not play as before, went to New York in the Depression and died there.

segments.title: Tio's composing and drinking
segments.summary: Tio was writing compositions, but drank heavily, missing lessons.

segments.title: Tio's father and uncle; Papa Tio's dislike of jazz
segments.summary: He remembers the older Tio, his softer tone, and the old man's disdain for jazz.

segments.title: The original Tuxedo band
segments.summary: Lineup of the Tuxedo band from 1910 as seen in Ridgely's photograph, and later members.

segments.title: Zutty's uncle Willie Bontemps and clarinetist Jimmie Noone
segments.summary: Russell asks about Zutty and Jimmie Noone; Cottrell knows Noone only by records and a 1937 meeting.

segments.title: Pianist Wilhelmina Barth and how to reach her
segments.summary: She played with Jimmie Noone and many others; Cottrell gives her name and spelling.

segments.title: Scheduling the interview and his job
segments.summary: He explains why interview was delayed and that he works on commission.

segments.title: Six months on the C clarinet before switching to B flat
segments.summary: Tio kept him on the C clarinet for six months before he moved to B flat.

segments.title: Embouchure, reed strength and Tio's own reed
segments.summary: Tio taught lip over bottom teeth and upper teeth on the mouthpiece but allowed variation; reeds varied.

segments.title: Tio's Buffet clarinet and his own B flat clarinet
segments.summary: Tio used a 13-key Buffet; Cottrell's father bought the B flat clarinet he still plays.

segments.title: Mouthpiece from Barney Bigard and study with him
segments.summary: Bigard gave him a mouthpiece in 1933 and taught him while Tio was away in New York.

segments.title: Tio's method of keeping time with the foot
segments.summary: Tio taught foot-tapping for time, then to feel it internally.

segments.title: Creole and French speech in his father's home
segments.summary: Aside on imitation of Tio and his father speaking Creole at home.

segments.title: Tio's stress on tone
segments.summary: Tio stressed getting a nice tone.
